name: length
use: Returns the length of this string, which is equal to the number of 16-bit Unicode characters (code units) contained in the sequence. If the string is empty (" "), returns 0. For supplementary Unicode characters (e.g., emojis), each surrogate pair counts as 2 code units toward this length.
example:
String s = "Barrackpore";
System.out.println("Length: " + s.length());
notes: length is a method in String (s.length()), whereas length is a field on Java arrays (arr.length).

name: isEmpty
use: Returns true if, and only if, length() is 0. Unlike isBlank(), a string containing one or more whitespace characters (e.g. " ") returns false.
notes: Always verify that the string reference is not null before invoking isEmpty(), or use Objects.requireNonNullElse(str, "").isEmpty().

name: isBlank
use: Returns true if the string is empty or contains only white space code points according to Character.isWhitespace(int). Handles all Unicode white spaces (including non-breaking spaces, em spaces, tabs, and line breaks).
exampleOutput:
s1 isBlank: true
s2 isBlank: false
notes: Prefer isBlank() over custom trim().isEmpty() checks, as isBlank() avoids allocating temporary stripped string instances on the heap.

name: charAt

arguments.name: index
arguments.description: The zero-based index of the char value to retrieve (0 <= index < length())

use: Returns the 16-bit char value at the specified zero-based index. Throws IndexOutOfBoundsException if the index is negative or not less than the length of this string.
exampleOutput:
First char: M
Last char: r
notes: Strings do not support array indexing syntax (s[0] is illegal in Java). Always use s.charAt(index).

name: codePointAt

arguments.name: index
arguments.description: The index to the char values (Unicode code units)

use: Returns the character (Unicode code point) at the specified index. If the char value at the given index is in the high-surrogate range and the following index is in the low-surrogate range, the supplementary 32-bit code point is returned.
notes: Essential when building internationalized software handling emojis, mathematical symbols, and historic Asian scripts.

name: codePointBefore

arguments.name: index
arguments.description: The index following the code point that should be returned (1 <= index <= length())

use: Returns the character (Unicode code point) before the specified index. If the char value at index - 1 is a low surrogate and index - 2 is a high surrogate, the combined supplementary code point is returned.
example:
String s = "Java";
System.out.println("Before index 1: " + (char) s.codePointBefore(1));
notes: Throws IndexOutOfBoundsException if index is less than 1 or greater than length().

name: codePointCount
signature: public int codePointCount(int beginIndex, int endIndex)

arguments.name: beginIndex
arguments.description: The index to the first char of the text range

arguments.name: endIndex
arguments.description: The index after the last char of the text range

use: Returns the number of Unicode code points in the specified text range of this String. Text with surrogate pairs (like emojis) has fewer code points than code units (length).
notes: Use codePointCount to calculate true character counts for user-facing text length constraints.

name: offsetByCodePoints
signature: public int offsetByCodePoints(int index, int codePointOffset)

arguments.name: index
arguments.description: The starting index

arguments.name: codePointOffset
arguments.description: The offset in code points

use: Returns the index within this String that is offset from the given index by codePointOffset code points. Unpaired surrogates within the text range count as one code point each.
notes: Crucial for stepping through strings with mixed ASCII and 4-byte Unicode characters without splitting surrogate pairs.

name: indexOf

arguments.name: ch
arguments.description: A character (Unicode code point)

use: Returns the index of the first occurrence of the character in this string. Returns -1 if the character does not occur.
notes: The parameter is an int (accepts char via widening conversion, or any 32-bit Unicode code point).

name: indexOf
signature: public int indexOf(int ch, int fromIndex)

arguments.name: ch
arguments.description: A character (Unicode code point)

arguments.name: fromIndex
arguments.description: The index to start the search from

use: Returns the index of the first occurrence of the character in this string at or after fromIndex. If fromIndex is negative, the entire string is searched (treated as 0). If fromIndex is greater than length, -1 is returned.
notes: Ideal for iterating through a string to find all occurrences of a delimiter or character.

name: indexOf

arguments.name: str
arguments.description: The substring to search for

use: Returns the index within this string of the first occurrence of the specified substring. Returns -1 if the substring does not occur. If str is empty (" "), returns 0.
example:
String s = "Spring Boot Java";
System.out.println("Index of 'Boot': " + s.indexOf("Boot"));
notes: Case-sensitive comparison. Use toLowerCase() on both strings or regex Pattern with CASE_INSENSITIVE for case-insensitive search.

name: indexOf
signature: public int indexOf(String str, int fromIndex)

arguments.name: str
arguments.description: The substring to search for

arguments.name: fromIndex
arguments.description: The index to start searching forward from

use: Returns the index of the first occurrence of the substring starting at the specified index. If fromIndex >= length(), returns -1 (unless str is empty, which returns length()).
example:
String s = "one fish two fish";
System.out.println("Second 'fish': " + s.indexOf("fish", 5));
notes: Internally uses vectorized intrinsics in HotSpot JVM for fast linear search.

name: lastIndexOf

arguments.name: ch
arguments.description: A character (Unicode code point)

use: Returns the index of the last occurrence of the character in this string, searching backwards starting from length() - 1. Returns -1 if the character is not found.
notes: Commonly used for parsing file extensions, URLs, and trailing directory delimiters.

name: lastIndexOf
signature: public int lastIndexOf(int ch, int fromIndex)

arguments.name: ch
arguments.description: A character (Unicode code point)

arguments.name: fromIndex
arguments.description: The index to start searching backward from

use: Returns the index of the last occurrence of the character, searching backwards starting at the specified index fromIndex. If fromIndex >= length(), searches from length() - 1. If fromIndex < 0, returns -1.
example:
String s = "banana";
System.out.println("Last 'a' before index 4: " + s.lastIndexOf('a', 4));
notes: Searches from right to left starting from fromIndex.

name: lastIndexOf

arguments.name: str
arguments.description: The substring to search for

use: Returns the index of the rightmost occurrence of the specified substring. Returns -1 if not found. If str is empty, returns length().
notes: Often paired with substring(lastSlash + 1) to extract the basename of a path.

name: lastIndexOf
signature: public int lastIndexOf(String str, int fromIndex)

arguments.name: str
arguments.description: The substring to search for

arguments.name: fromIndex
arguments.description: The index to start the backward search from

use: Returns the index of the rightmost occurrence of the specified substring at or before fromIndex.
example:
String s = "cat dog cat dog";
System.out.println("Match: " + s.lastIndexOf("cat", 10));
notes: Throws NullPointerException if str is null.

name: contains

arguments.name: s
arguments.description: The sequence to search for (e.g. String, StringBuilder)

use: Returns true if and only if this string contains the specified sequence of char values. Equivalent to indexOf(s.toString()) >= 0. Case-sensitive.
exampleOutput:
Has AccoTax: true
Has Python: false
notes: Accepts any CharSequence, meaning you can pass a StringBuilder or StringBuffer directly without converting to String first.

name: startsWith

arguments.name: prefix
arguments.description: The prefix to test

use: Tests if this string starts with the specified prefix. Returns true if the character sequence represented by the argument is a prefix of this string; false otherwise. Always returns true if prefix is empty.
example:
String url = "https://www.codernaccotax.co.in";
System.out.println("Secure URL: " + url.startsWith("https://"));
notes: Case-sensitive comparison. Faster than regex or substring comparisons.

name: startsWith
signature: public boolean startsWith(String prefix, int toOffset)

arguments.name: prefix
arguments.description: The prefix to test

arguments.name: toOffset
arguments.description: Where to begin looking in this string

use: Tests if the substring of this string beginning at the specified index starts with the specified prefix. Returns false if toOffset is negative or greater than length().
example:
String s = "order-REF-10029";
System.out.println("Has REF at 6: " + s.startsWith("REF", 6));
notes: Avoids creating a substring before calling startsWith, saving heap allocation.

name: endsWith

arguments.name: suffix
arguments.description: The suffix to test

use: Tests if this string ends with the specified suffix. Equivalent to startsWith(suffix, length() - suffix.length()). Always returns true if suffix is empty.
example:
String file = "Resume.pdf";
System.out.println("Is PDF: " + file.endsWith(".pdf"));
notes: Case-sensitive. If you need case-insensitive suffix checking, use file.toLowerCase().endsWith(".pdf").

name: matches

arguments.name: regex
arguments.description: The regular expression to which this string is to be matched

use: Tells whether or not this string matches the given regular expression. Compiles the regex and checks Pattern.matches(regex, str). Matches the ENTIRE string, not just a subsequence.
exampleOutput:
Valid 6-digit PIN: true
Alpha match: false
notes: Compiles Pattern on every call. In performance-critical code or loops, precompile with Pattern.compile(regex) instead.

name: equals

arguments.name: anObject
arguments.description: The object to compare this String against

use: Compares this string to the specified object. The result is true if and only if the argument is not null and is a String object that represents the same sequence of characters as this object. Reference equality (==) is checked first for high speed.
notes: Always use "CONSTANT".equals(variable) to avoid NullPointerException when the variable might be null.

name: equalsIgnoreCase

arguments.name: anotherString
arguments.description: The String to compare this String against

use: Compares this String to another String, ignoring case considerations. Two strings are considered equal if they are of the same length and corresponding characters are equal ignoring case. Returns false if anotherString is null.
notes: Faster and more memory-friendly than s1.toLowerCase().equals(s2.toLowerCase()), because it avoids creating temporary string copies.

name: contentEquals

arguments.name: cs
arguments.description: The sequence to compare this String against (e.g., StringBuffer, StringBuilder, CharBuffer)

use: Compares this string to the specified CharSequence. Returns true if and only if this String represents the same sequence of char values as the specified sequence. Synchronizes if cs is a StringBuffer.
notes: Essential because String.equals() always returns false when passed a StringBuilder.

name: contentEquals

arguments.name: sb
arguments.description: The StringBuffer to compare this String against

use: Specialized overload for StringBuffer that synchronizes on the buffer to ensure thread-safe content inspection.
notes: Thread-safe when comparing against a shared StringBuffer instance.

name: compareTo

arguments.name: anotherString
arguments.description: The String to be compared

use: Compares two strings lexicographically based on the Unicode value of each character. Returns 0 if equal, a negative integer if this string lexicographically precedes the argument, or a positive integer if this string follows it. Implements Comparable<String>.
notes: If one string is a prefix of another, returns the difference in lengths (this.length() - anotherString.length()).

name: compareToIgnoreCase

arguments.name: str
arguments.description: The String to be compared

use: Compares two strings lexicographically, ignoring case differences. Normalized using Character.toLowerCase(Character.toUpperCase(character)).
notes: Commonly passed as a comparator (String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER) to sort lists or arrays ignoring case.

name: regionMatches
signature: public boolean regionMatches(int toffset, String other, int ooffset, int len)

arguments.name: toffset
arguments.description: The starting offset of the subregion in this string

arguments.name: other
arguments.description: The string argument

arguments.name: ooffset
arguments.description: The starting offset of the subregion in the string argument

arguments.name: len
arguments.description: The number of characters to compare

use: Tests if two string regions are equal. A substring of this String object is compared to a substring of the argument other. Returns false if any offset is negative or out of bounds.
notes: Compares subregions without creating intermediate substring objects, making it very memory efficient.

name: regionMatches
signature: public boolean regionMatches(boolean ignoreCase, int toffset, String other, int ooffset, int len)

arguments.name: ignoreCase
arguments.description: If true, ignore case when comparing characters

arguments.name: toffset
arguments.description: The starting offset in this string

arguments.name: other
arguments.description: The other string argument

arguments.name: ooffset
arguments.description: The starting offset in the other string

arguments.name: len
arguments.description: The number of characters to compare

use: Tests if two string regions are equal, with optional case insensitivity.
notes: Provides zero-allocation case-insensitive partial substring comparisons.

name: substring

arguments.name: beginIndex
arguments.description: The beginning index, inclusive (0 <= beginIndex <= length())

use: Returns a string that is a substring of this string. The substring begins with the character at the specified index and extends to the end of this string.
example:
String s = "Kolkata";
System.out.println("Sub: " + s.substring(3));
notes: If beginIndex is 0, returns 'this' exact reference without creating a new object on HotSpot JVM.

name: substring
signature: public String substring(int beginIndex, int endIndex)

arguments.name: beginIndex
arguments.description: The beginning index, inclusive

arguments.name: endIndex
arguments.description: The ending index, exclusive

use: Returns a string that is a substring of this string. The substring begins at the specified beginIndex and extends to the character at index endIndex - 1. Thus the length of the substring is endIndex - beginIndex.
example:
String s = "Barrackpore";
System.out.println("Slice: " + s.substring(0, 8));
notes: Throws IndexOutOfBoundsException if beginIndex < 0, endIndex > length(), or beginIndex > endIndex.

name: subSequence
signature: public CharSequence subSequence(int beginIndex, int endIndex)

arguments.name: beginIndex
arguments.description: The beginning index, inclusive

arguments.name: endIndex
arguments.description: The ending index, exclusive

use: Returns a new character sequence that is a subsequence of this sequence. An invocation of this method of the form str.subSequence(begin, end) behaves in exactly the same way as str.substring(begin, end). Implements CharSequence.
example:
CharSequence cs = "Enterprise";
System.out.println(cs.subSequence(0, 5));
notes: Useful when writing generalized algorithms that operate on any CharSequence.

name: toLowerCase
use: Converts all characters in this String to lower case using the rules of the default locale. If no characters in the string need conversion, returns 'this' original string.
example:
String s = "JAVA CORE";
System.out.println(s.toLowerCase());
notes: In international apps, prefer toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT) to prevent locale-specific casing anomalies.

name: toLowerCase

arguments.name: locale
arguments.description: Use the case transformation rules for this locale

use: Converts all characters in this String to lower case using the rules of the given Locale.
example:
String s = "TITLE";
System.out.println(s.toLowerCase(java.util.Locale.ROOT));
notes: Locale.ROOT provides uniform, predictable ASCII case conversions across all operating systems.

name: toUpperCase
use: Converts all characters in this String to upper case using the rules of the default locale.
example:
String s = "sukanta hui";
System.out.println(s.toUpperCase());
notes: String immutability means s remains unchanged; you must reassign or consume the return value.

name: toUpperCase

arguments.name: locale
arguments.description: Use the case transformation rules for this locale

use: Converts all characters in this String to upper case using the rules of the given Locale.
example:
String s = "invoice";
System.out.println(s.toUpperCase(java.util.Locale.ENGLISH));
notes: Always pass a locale when building protocol parsers or database identifiers.

name: trim
use: Returns a string whose value is this string, with all leading and trailing space removed, where space is defined as any character whose code point is less than or equal to 'U+0020' (the ASCII space).
example:
String s = "  Hello World  ";
System.out.println("[" + s.trim() + "]");
notes: Does not remove full Unicode whitespace (like non-breaking space \u00A0). Use strip() in Java 11+ for Unicode.

name: strip
use: Returns a string whose value is this string, with all leading and trailing white space removed. Unicode-aware: uses Character.isWhitespace(int).
example:
String s = "\u2005 Java 21 \u2005";
System.out.println("[" + s.strip() + "]");
notes: Modern replacement for trim(). Handles all Unicode whitespace characters correctly.

name: stripLeading
use: Returns a string whose value is this string, with all leading white space removed. Leaves trailing whitespace intact.
example:
String s = "   indented text   ";
System.out.println("[" + s.stripLeading() + "]");
notes: Ideal for parsing code blocks or indented configuration text lines.

name: stripTrailing
use: Returns a string whose value is this string, with all trailing white space removed. Leaves leading whitespace intact.
example:
String s = "   indented text   ";
System.out.println("[" + s.stripTrailing() + "]");
notes: Great for cleaning up trailing spaces in source code formatters.

name: stripIndent
use: Returns a string whose value is this string, with incidental white space removed from the beginning and end of every line. Computes the minimal common indentation of all lines and strips that amount from each line.
example:
String block = "    line 1\n    line 2";
System.out.println(block.stripIndent());
notes: Designed to support Java 15+ Text Blocks (triple quotes """).

name: translateEscapes
use: Returns a string whose value is this string, with escape sequences (such as \b, \t, \n, \f, \r, \", \', and \\) translated as if in a string literal.
example:
String raw = "Hello\\nWorld";
System.out.println(raw.translateEscapes());
notes: Useful when parsing raw escape sequences from config files or JSON strings.

name: indent

arguments.name: n
arguments.description: Number of leading white space characters to add (if positive) or remove (if negative) per line

use: Adjusts the indentation of each line of this string based on the value of n, and normalizes line termination characters to \n.
example:
String s = "Line 1\nLine 2";
System.out.print(s.indent(2));
notes: Passing a negative integer removes up to |n| leading whitespace characters from each line.

name: repeat

arguments.name: count
arguments.description: Number of times to repeat (>= 0)

use: Returns a string whose value is the concatenation of this string repeated count times. If count == 0 or the string is empty, returns an empty string. Throws IllegalArgumentException if count < 0.
example:
String sep = "=".repeat(10);
System.out.println(sep);
notes: Much faster than StringBuilder loops for generating repeated headers, dividers, and padding.

name: transform
signature: public <R> R transform(Function<? super String, ? extends R> f)

arguments.name: f
arguments.description: The transformation function to apply

use: Allows the application of a function to this string. The function should expect a single String argument and produce an R result. Enables fluent pipeline chaining on String instances.
notes: Eliminates intermediate variables in functional method chaining pipelines.

name: replace
signature: public String replace(char oldChar, char newChar)

arguments.name: oldChar
arguments.description: The old character to be replaced

arguments.name: newChar
arguments.description: The new character to replace it with

use: Returns a string resulting from replacing all occurrences of oldChar in this string with newChar. If oldChar does not occur, 'this' exact reference is returned.
example:
String s = "mesquite in your cellar";
System.out.println(s.replace('e', 'o'));
notes: Fast character replacement without regex compilation.

name: replace
signature: public String replace(CharSequence target, CharSequence replacement)

arguments.name: target
arguments.description: The sequence of char values to be replaced

arguments.name: replacement
arguments.description: The replacement sequence of char values

use: Replaces each substring of this string that matches the literal target sequence with the specified literal replacement sequence. Replacement proceeds from the beginning of the string to the end.
example:
String ip = "192.168.1.1";
System.out.println(ip.replace(".", "-"));
notes: Unlike replaceAll(), replace() treats dots and special characters as literal text, NOT regular expressions!

name: replaceAll
signature: public String replaceAll(String regex, String replacement)

arguments.name: regex
arguments.description: The regular expression to which this string is to be matched

arguments.name: replacement
arguments.description: The string to be substituted for each match (supports $1, $2 capture groups)

use: Replaces each substring of this string that matches the given regular expression with the given replacement. Supports regex capture group backreferences ($1, $2, etc.).
notes: Throws PatternSyntaxException if regex syntax is invalid. To escape special characters in replacement, use Matcher.quoteReplacement().

name: replaceFirst
signature: public String replaceFirst(String regex, String replacement)

arguments.name: regex
arguments.description: The regular expression to match

arguments.name: replacement
arguments.description: The replacement string for the first match

use: Replaces the first substring of this string that matches the given regular expression with the given replacement.
example:
String s = "red car, red boat, red house";
System.out.println(s.replaceFirst("red", "blue"));
exampleOutput: blue car, red boat, red house
notes: Stops immediately after substituting the first match, saving regex execution time.

name: split

arguments.name: regex
arguments.description: The delimiting regular expression

use: Splits this string around matches of the given regular expression. Trailing empty strings are not included in the resulting array (equivalent to split(regex, 0)).
notes: Pitfall: "a,b,,".split(",") produces an array of length 2, discarding the trailing empty strings.

name: split
signature: public String[] split(String regex, int limit)

arguments.name: regex
arguments.description: The delimiting regular expression

arguments.name: limit
arguments.description: The result threshold (positive = max tokens; negative = keep all trailing blanks; 0 = discard trailing blanks)

use: Splits this string around matches of the given regular expression. If limit > 0, pattern is applied at most limit - 1 times. If limit < 0, trailing empty strings are preserved. If limit == 0, trailing empty strings are discarded.
notes: Pass limit = -1 when parsing CSV lines to preserve trailing empty cells!

name: splitWithDelimiters
signature: public String[] splitWithDelimiters(String regex, int limit)

arguments.name: regex
arguments.description: The delimiting regular expression

arguments.name: limit
arguments.description: The result threshold

use: Splits this string around matches of the given regular expression and returns both the tokens and the matching delimiters in the resulting array.
notes: Modern addition in Java 21 for building mathematical and domain-specific tokenizers.

name: join
signature: public static String join(CharSequence delimiter, CharSequence... elements)

arguments.name: delimiter
arguments.description: The delimiter that separates each element

arguments.name: elements
arguments.description: The elements to join together

use: Returns a new String composed of copies of the CharSequence elements joined together with a copy of the specified delimiter. If an element is null, "null" is added.
example:
String path = String.join("/", "usr", "local", "bin");
System.out.println(path);
notes: Static factory method. Does not add leading or trailing delimiters.

name: join
signature: public static String join(CharSequence delimiter, Iterable<? extends CharSequence> elements)

arguments.name: delimiter
arguments.description: A sequence of characters that is used to separate each of the elements

arguments.name: elements
arguments.description: An Iterable that will have its elements joined together (e.g. List<String>)

use: Returns a new String composed of copies of the elements of an Iterable joined together with the specified delimiter.
example:
java.util.List<String> list = java.util.List.of("Java", "Spring", "Docker");
System.out.println(String.join(" -> ", list));
notes: Internally uses java.util.StringJoiner for optimal performance.

name: toCharArray
use: Converts this string to a newly allocated character array. Its length is the length of this string and its contents are initialized to contain the character sequence represented by this string.
notes: Because toCharArray() returns a defensive copy, mutating the returned array cannot violate String immutability.

name: getBytes
use: Encodes this String into a sequence of bytes using the platform's default charset, storing the result into a new byte array.
example:
byte[] bytes = "Hello".getBytes();
System.out.println("Byte count: " + bytes.length);
notes: Avoid using parameterless getBytes() in cross-platform or network apps; always supply an explicit Charset (StandardCharsets.UTF_8).

name: getBytes

arguments.name: charset
arguments.description: The java.nio.charset.Charset to be used to encode the String

use: Encodes this String into a sequence of bytes using the given Charset, storing the result into a new byte array.
example:
byte[] utf8Bytes = "Barrackpore".getBytes(java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
System.out.println("UTF-8 Bytes: " + utf8Bytes.length);
notes: StandardCharsets.UTF_8 is preferred because it never throws UnsupportedEncodingException.

name: getChars
signature: public void getChars(int srcBegin, int srcEnd, char[] dst, int dstBegin)

arguments.name: srcBegin
arguments.description: Index of the first character in the string to copy

arguments.name: srcEnd
arguments.description: Index after the last character in the string to copy

arguments.name: dst
arguments.description: The destination array

arguments.name: dstBegin
arguments.description: The start offset in the destination array

use: Copies characters from this string into the destination character array without allocating a new array.
notes: Zero-allocation batch copying method used heavily in high-performance parsers.

name: intern
use: Returns a canonical representation for the string object. When intern() is invoked, if the String Constant Pool already contains a string equal to this String object (as determined by equals()), then the string from the pool is returned. Otherwise, this String object is added to the pool and a reference to it is returned.
exampleOutput:
s1 == s3: false
s2 == s3: true
notes: Since Java 7, the SCP is located in the main Heap. Interning identical strings across millions of records dramatically reduces memory footprints.

name: hashCode
use: Returns a hash code for this string. The hash code for a String object is computed as: s[0]*31^(n-1) + s[1]*31^(n-2) + ... + s[n-1] using int arithmetic. The calculated hash is cached in an internal field so it is calculated at most once.
example:
String s = "Java";
System.out.println("Hash: " + s.hashCode());
notes: Because Strings are immutable, the cached hash code never changes, making String the most optimal and secure key for HashMaps.

name: toString
use: Returns this string itself (returns 'this').
example:
String s = "Hello";
System.out.println(s == s.toString());
notes: Overridden from Object. Returns the exact reference itself without allocating a copy.

name: format
signature: public static String format(String format, Object... args)

arguments.name: format
arguments.description: A format string with specifiers (%s, %d, %f, etc.)

arguments.name: args
arguments.description: Arguments referenced by the format specifiers

use: Returns a formatted string using the specified format string and arguments with the default locale. Delegates to java.util.Formatter.
example:
String res = String.format("Item: %s | Price: $%.2f | Qty: %d", "Laptop", 1299.99, 2);
System.out.println(res);
notes: Produces high-precision numbers, padded strings, and formatted dates cleanly.

name: formatted

arguments.name: args
arguments.description: Arguments referenced by the format specifiers in this string

use: Formats using this string as the format string, and the supplied arguments. Equivalent to String.format(this, args). Instance method convenience.
example:
String template = "Student: %s, Marks: %d";
System.out.println(template.formatted("Rahul", 95));
notes: Syntactic sugar introduced in Java 15, frequently paired with Text Blocks.

name: valueOf

arguments.name: obj
arguments.description: An Object to convert

use: Returns the string representation of the Object argument. If the argument is null, then a string equal to "null" is returned; otherwise, the value of obj.toString() is returned.
example:
Object obj = null;
System.out.println("Safe valueOf: " + String.valueOf(obj));
notes: Null-safe alternative to calling obj.toString().

name: valueOf

arguments.name: data
arguments.description: The character array

use: Returns the string representation of the char array argument. The contents of the character array are copied; subsequent modification of the character array does not affect the newly created string.
notes: WARNING: Passing (char[]) null triggers NullPointerException, unlike valueOf(Object)!

name: valueOf
signature: public static String valueOf(char[] data, int offset, int count)

arguments.name: data
arguments.description: The character array

arguments.name: offset
arguments.description: Initial offset into the char array

arguments.name: count
arguments.description: Length of the subarray

use: Returns the string representation of a specific subarray of the char array argument.
example:
char[] letters = {'a', 'b', 'c', 'd', 'e'};
System.out.println(String.valueOf(letters, 1, 3));
notes: Copies only count characters starting from offset into a new String.

name: valueOf

arguments.name: i
arguments.description: An int value

use: Returns the string representation of the int argument. Equivalent to Integer.toString(i).
example:
String s = String.valueOf(2026);
System.out.println("Year: " + s);
notes: Faster than "" + i because it avoids temporary StringBuilder or invokedynamic overhead.

name: valueOf

arguments.name: d
arguments.description: A double value

use: Returns the string representation of the double argument via Double.toString(d). Handles NaN and Infinity.
example:
String s = String.valueOf(3.14159);
System.out.println("Pi: " + s);
notes: Correctly outputs NaN, Infinity, -Infinity, and scientific notation where applicable.

name: valueOf

arguments.name: b
arguments.description: A boolean value

use: Returns "true" if the argument is true, or "false" if the argument is false. Returns pooled literals directly.
example:
boolean status = true;
System.out.println(String.valueOf(status));
notes: Zero allocation: returns the canonical pooled "true" or "false" literal.

name: copyValueOf

arguments.name: data
arguments.description: The character array

use: Equivalent to String.valueOf(char[]). Retained for backwards compatibility with early Java editions.
example:
char[] chars = {'J', 'a', 'v', 'a'};
System.out.println(String.copyValueOf(chars));
notes: Historical synonym for valueOf(char[]).

name: lines
use: Returns a Stream of lines extracted from this string, separated by line terminators (\n, \r, \r\n). Lazily evaluated.
notes: Far more memory-efficient than split("\n") on massive multiline strings because it produces a lazy stream.

name: chars
use: Returns an IntStream of char values from this sequence. Any char which maps to a surrogate code point is passed through uninterpreted. Implements CharSequence.
notes: Returns an IntStream because Java primitives byte, short, char do not have dedicated stream types.

name: codePoints
use: Returns an IntStream of code point values from this sequence. Any surrogate pairs encountered in the sequence are combined into single 32-bit Unicode code points.
example:
String s = "A😀B";
System.out.println("Total code points: " + s.codePoints().count());
notes: Proper way to process modern strings with emojis or extended multilingual scripts using the Stream API.
